title: The Small Shop
author: Barashada Ingiriisiga
description: A couple's small grocery shop faces a rent increase, a dishonest supplier, and a new competitor, and they must make smart decisions to keep their business alive.

chapters.title: A New Beginning
chapters.text:
Amina stood back and looked at the small shop. The white walls were clean, and the shelves were full of bright packets and tins. The smell of fresh bread and coffee came from the back. It was a good smell. It was the smell of a new beginning.

Omar came to stand beside her. He put his arm around her shoulder. "Well," he said. "This is it. Our shop."

Amina smiled. She felt a mix of excitement and fear in her stomach. "It's ours, Omar. All ours."

They had worked for other people for many years. Omar had driven a taxi, and Amina had worked in a hotel kitchen. They had saved their money, a little bit at a time, for a long time. They had a dream, and the dream was this: a small grocery shop in a busy part of the city. A place where people could buy their daily needs - milk, bread, eggs, rice, and soap. A place where they could be their own bosses.

The shop was not big, but it was in a good position. It was on a corner, near a bus stop and a small park. Many people passed by every day. Amina and Omar knew that a good position was very important for a shop.

Their first week was very busy. They worked from early morning until late at night. They learned the names of their customers. There was Mr. Chen, who bought a newspaper and a bottle of water every morning. There was Mrs. Petrova, who always asked for the freshest vegetables. And there were the school children who came in the afternoon to buy sweets and cold drinks.

"Hello, Mr. Chen!" Omar would call out when the old man came in. "The newspaper is here, and your water is cold."

Mr. Chen would nod and smile. "Good service, Omar. You and your wife are doing a good job."

These small words of praise made Omar and Amina very happy. They worked hard to make sure the shop was always clean and tidy. They checked the prices at other shops to make sure their prices were fair. They listened to their customers and tried to get the things they wanted.

After two months, the shop was doing well. They were not rich, but they were making a small profit. They could pay for the goods from their suppliers and have a little money left for themselves. For the first time in their lives, they felt secure. They felt that they were building something for their future.

One evening, after they had closed the shop, they sat at the small table in the back room. They were counting the day's money. Amina was writing numbers in a small notebook.

"Look at this, Omar," she said, pointing to a number. "This is our best day yet."

Omar smiled. "That's wonderful, Amina. Our hard work is paying off. Maybe next year, we can even think about hiring someone to help us."

"Maybe," Amina said, but her voice was tired. "But first, we need to talk about the rent. It takes a lot of our money every month."

Omar's smile disappeared. He knew the rent was high. The landlord, Mr. Haddad, was a serious man who owned many buildings in the area. He had been fair to them at the beginning, but Omar often worried about the future.

"We have a contract for one year," Omar said. "The price cannot change for one year."

"I know," Amina said. "But after that, who knows?"

They finished their work and turned off the lights. They walked home together, their hands touching. The night air was cool and clean. They were tired, but they were happy.

A few days later, a letter arrived at the shop. It was from Mr. Haddad, the landlord. Amina opened it with a strange feeling in her heart. She read the letter quickly, then read it again. Her face became pale.

"Omar," she said, her voice shaking. "Omar, look at this."

Omar took the letter from her hand. He read it slowly. The letter was polite and formal. It said that Mr. Haddad was happy that they were good tenants. It said that the area was becoming more popular, and the value of the building was going up. Because of this, the rent for the shop would increase. The new rent would be twenty percent higher than the current price. This new price would start in three months.

Omar's hand holding the letter dropped to his side. He looked at Amina, and he saw the same fear in her eyes that he felt in his heart. Twenty percent. That was a lot of money. It was almost all of their profit.

"We cannot pay this," Amina said quietly. "We will lose the shop."

Omar did not answer. He just looked at the letter in his hand. The dream that they had worked so hard for suddenly felt very fragile. It was like a small flame in the wind. They had a difficult decision to make. They had to find a way to keep their business alive.

chapters.title: Trouble with the Supplier
chapters.text:
Amina and Omar sat at the small table in the back of their shop. On the table was the letter from their landlord, Mr. Haddad. The letter said that the rent would go up by twenty percent from next month. Amina looked at Omar. "We have to talk to him," she said. Omar nodded. "We can't afford this increase. Our profit is already very small."

They closed the shop early that afternoon and walked to Mr. Haddad's office. The office was on the second floor of an old building. Mr. Haddad was a large man with a thick grey moustache. He smiled when he saw them, but the smile did not reach his eyes.

"Mr. Haddad," Omar began, "we have been good tenants. We always pay on time. Can we discuss the rent increase?"

Mr. Haddad leaned back in his chair. "The market is going up, Omar. The value of this property is rising. I must ask for a fair price."

Amina spoke. "But twenty percent is a lot. We are a small shop. We cannot pass this cost to our customers. They will go to the big supermarket."

Mr. Haddad shook his head. "I have to think about my own investment. I am sorry, but the new rent is final. If you cannot pay, I will need to find another tenant."

Omar felt his hands get cold. He looked at Amina. She looked tired. "Please, Mr. Haddad, can we meet halfway? Ten percent?" Omar asked.

Mr. Haddad stood up. "My decision is final. You have one month to decide. I hope you stay, but I must be practical."

They walked out of the office in silence. The sun was hot on the street. Omar put his hand on Amina's shoulder. "We will find a way," he said, but his voice did not sound sure.

Back at the shop, they found a delivery truck outside. Their usual supplier, a company called "Fresh Foods," had sent a new order. The driver was unloading boxes. Amina signed the delivery note.

They started to unpack the boxes. Amina opened a box of apples. She stopped. The apples were small and had brown spots. She opened another box of oranges. Many of them were soft. Omar opened a carton of milk. He looked at the date. It was only three days until it expired.

"This is not good quality," Amina said. "This is not what we ordered."

Omar looked at the invoice. He compared it with the price list they had. "Wait," he said. "Look at this. The price for rice has gone up by five percent. And the price for cooking oil is higher too. But they didn't tell us."

Amina's face went white. "They are cheating us. We have been loyal customers for two years."

Omar felt a mix of anger and worry. "First the landlord, now this. Our costs are going up, and our products are worse. We are losing money every day."

They sat on the boxes. Amina started to make a list. "We need to find a new supplier," she said. "But we have to be careful. We need someone reliable, with good prices and good quality."

Omar agreed. "We cannot trust Fresh Foods anymore. We have to search."

That evening, they did not watch TV. They used their old laptop and searched for local wholesalers. They made phone calls. They wrote down names and addresses.

The next morning, they visited a wholesale market on the other side of the city. The market was big and noisy. Many small shop owners were buying fruit, vegetables, and dry goods. Amina and Omar walked between the stalls. They asked about prices. They compared the quality.

At one stall, a woman named Mrs. Khalil was selling fresh vegetables. The tomatoes were red and firm. The lettuce was green and crisp. Amina asked, "How much for a box of tomatoes?"

Mrs. Khalil told her the price. Amina looked at Omar. It was ten percent cheaper than Fresh Foods. And the quality was much better.

They talked to Mrs. Khalil. She explained that she worked with local farmers. "No middlemen," she said. "That is why my prices are fair."

Omar asked about delivery. Mrs. Khalil said she could deliver twice a week. She gave them a price list. There were no hidden fees.

Amina and Omar looked at each other. This seemed perfect. But they were cautious. "Can we try a small order first?" Omar asked.

"Of course," Mrs. Khalil said with a smile. "I want to build a long relationship with you."

They placed a small order for vegetables and fruit. They decided to keep using Fresh Foods for some dry goods for now, but they would test Mrs. Khalil's service.

As they drove back to the shop, Omar felt a little lighter. "This is good, Amina. We have a new option."

Amina nodded. "But we still have the rent problem. We need to increase our sales. We cannot just reduce costs."

Omar thought. "Maybe we can offer special deals. Or we can start selling fresh bread in the morning. People love fresh bread."

Amina smiled for the first time that day. "That is a good idea. We can work together."

They parked outside their shop. The sign "Amina & Omar's Grocery" looked a little old. But they had new hope. They knew they had to work hard, but they were ready to fight for their small shop.

chapters.title: A New Competitor
chapters.text:
Amina was arranging oranges at the front of the shop when she saw the men across the street. They were carrying large signs and putting them in the window of the empty building. The signs were bright yellow and red. They said: "Fresh Market - Everything at Low Prices. Opening Soon!"

She called Omar immediately. He came from the back room, where he was checking the boxes from their new supplier. The new supplier had better prices and better quality, and Omar felt good about that change. But when he saw the signs, his face changed.

"That building has been empty for six months," he said slowly. "Who is opening a shop there?"

"I don't know," Amina said. "But look at the signs. Low prices. Many people in this neighborhood love low prices."

They watched from their door as the workers put more signs in the windows. One sign showed pictures of vegetables and meat with big red numbers under them. Omar could not see the numbers clearly, but he knew they would be low. Very low.

The next week, the new shop opened. Its name was Fresh Market, and it was big and bright inside. The owners had painted the walls white and put new shelves everywhere. On the first day, a long line of people waited outside before the doors opened.

Amina and Omar stood in their own shop and watched. Their shop was quiet. Only two customers came that morning. One was Mr. Hassan, an old man who lived nearby. He bought bread and milk, as he always did. The other was a young woman who bought only a bottle of water.

"This is bad," Omar said quietly. "Very bad."

That evening, they counted the money from the day. It was the worst day since they opened the shop. Amina looked at the numbers and felt a heavy weight in her chest.

"We cannot continue like this," she said. "If we lose our customers, we lose everything."

Omar agreed. They sat at the small table in the back room and talked about what to do.

"Maybe we should lower our prices," Omar said. "If we match their prices, customers will come back."

Amina shook her head. "We cannot. Our rent is going up, and we already pay a lot for good products. If we lower our prices too much, we will lose money on every sale. We are not a big company. We do not have the power to sell at very low prices."

Omar knew she was right. Fresh Market was part of a large group of shops. They could buy huge amounts of products, so their costs were lower. A small shop like theirs could never win a price war.

"Then what can we do?" Omar asked. "Do we just close the shop and find other jobs?"

"No," Amina said firmly. "We have worked too hard. We must think of other ideas."

They sat in silence for a moment. Then Amina spoke again.

"We cannot compete with them on price. But we can compete on other things. We can offer products that they do not have."

"What products?" Omar asked.

"We can find local producers," Amina said. "There are farmers outside the city who sell good vegetables and fruit. Their products are fresh, and they are not expensive. Fresh Market sells products from big factories. Many people want fresh, local food."

Omar thought about this. "That is a good idea. But it will take time to find these farmers and make agreements with them."

"Time is something we have," Amina said. "We just need to use it well."

"Also," Omar added, "we can offer something that Fresh Market cannot offer. We know our customers. We know their names, their families, their problems. When Mrs. Karim comes in, we ask about her son. When Mr. Ali comes in, we know he likes his coffee beans from a special place. Fresh Market does not know these people."

Amina smiled for the first time that day. "Yes. We can offer better service. We can help people carry their bags. We can remember their orders. We can be friendly and warm. A big shop cannot do that."

Omar nodded. "And we can also add some small things. We can sell fresh coffee at the front of the shop. People can sit and drink it while they talk. Nobody will do that in Fresh Market."

Amina wrote their ideas on a piece of paper. First: find local farmers and sell fresh products. Second: improve customer service and remember each customer's needs. Third: add a small coffee corner. Fourth: maybe offer home delivery for old people who cannot walk to the shop.

"We cannot do everything at once," she said. "We must choose what is most important."

"I think the coffee corner is easy to start," Omar said. "We already have a small machine from my uncle. We can buy good coffee beans and start next week."

"And the local farmers?" Amina asked.

"I will visit them on my day off," Omar said. "I know some farmers from my childhood village. They will help us."

They looked at the paper again. It was not a complete plan, but it was a start. They had ideas, and they had hope.

"We must be patient," Amina said. "Customers will not come back in one day. But if we give them good reasons, they will return."

Omar took her hand. "We will make this work. We have each other, and we have our little shop. That is enough."

Outside, the lights of Fresh Market were still bright across the street. But inside their small shop, Amina and Omar were making plans. They knew the road ahead would not be easy. But they were ready to try.

chapters.title: The Decision
chapters.text:
For two days, the shop felt quiet and sad. Amina stood behind the counter and watched the street. Across the road, the new discount store was busy. People carried big bags and smiled. She turned to Omar, who was putting old apples in a box.

"We cannot fight them on price," she said. "Their prices are too low. We will lose all our money."

Omar nodded. He looked tired. "So what do we do? We cannot just wait."

Amina picked up one of the apples. It was soft and had a brown spot. She put it down. "This is the problem," she said. "Our supplier sends us bad fruit. The customers see it and they leave. We need to change everything."

That evening, they sat at the small table behind the shop. They had paper and a pen. They wrote down their ideas. Lower prices? No. That was dangerous. Special products? Maybe, but what kind? Better service? Yes, but how?

Then Amina had an idea. She remembered the old market in her grandmother's town. People knew each other. They talked. The sellers knew their customers' names. It was not just about shopping. It was about community.

"We cannot be the cheapest shop," she said slowly. "But we can be the friendliest shop. We can be the shop that knows its customers. We can sell fresh, local food. Good food. We can make people feel welcome."

Omar thought about it. His face changed. A small smile appeared. "You mean, we stop trying to be like them?"

"Yes," Amina said. "We be different. We be ourselves."

They made a plan. First, they needed a new supplier. They called a small farm outside the city. The farm grew vegetables and fruit. It was not expensive, but the quality was good. The farmer, a woman named Rosa, agreed to deliver fresh produce three times a week. The prices were fair, and she was honest. Amina felt hope for the first time in weeks.

Second, they created a loyalty card. Every time a customer bought something, they got a stamp. After ten stamps, they received a free loaf of bread or a basket of fruit. It was simple, but it gave people a reason to come back.

Third, they decided to organize a small market day. They put a sign in the window: "Come to Our First Market Day - Saturday at 10am." Omar asked Rosa to bring extra vegetables. Amina baked cakes and bread. They bought some tables and put them outside the shop.

On Saturday, the sun was bright. Amina and Omar arrived early. They put the tables out and covered them with clean white cloths. Rosa arrived with boxes of tomatoes, green beans, and fresh herbs. The smell was wonderful.

At first, nobody came. Amina felt nervous. She looked across the street. The discount store was open, but it was quiet. Then, Mrs. Chen, an old woman from the building next door, walked over.

"What is this?" she asked, looking at the tables.

"It's a small market," Omar said. "Everything is from a local farm. Fresh today."

Mrs. Chen picked up a tomato. She smelled it. "This looks like my mother's garden," she said. She bought three.

Then more people came. A young man bought a bag of apples. A mother bought vegetables for soup. Amina talked to everyone. She remembered their names. She asked about their children. Omar gave free coffee to everyone who bought something.

Across the street, a man from the discount store watched. He shook his head. But he did not come over.

By the end of the day, the tables were nearly empty. Amina counted the money in the box. It was not a huge amount, but it was more than they had expected. More importantly, the shop felt full of life again.

A week later, Mrs. Chen came back. She had her friend with her. "I told her about your tomatoes," she said. "We want two boxes."

The new supplier made a big difference. The vegetables were fresh and tasty. Customers started to notice. They told their neighbors. The loyalty cards worked too. People brought them back and smiled when they got their free bread.

Amina and Omar did not become rich. They still worried about the rent increase. But they had a plan, and they had each other. They had learned something important: they could not compete with the big store, but they did not need to. They had something better - trust, quality, and a place where people felt at home.

Omar looked at Amina one evening as they closed the shop. "We made the right decision," he said.

Amina smiled. "We made our own decision," she said. "And that is the best one."
